Corrupted localStorage or API responses fail cleanly with actionable errors instead of NaN UI glitches.

commonMistakes.mistake: Casting `JSON.parse(str) as AppState` without checking keys
commonMistakes.fix: If a user has an older localStorage schema, missing fields cause silent runtime crashes; validate and merge defaults safely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Re-validating the same trusted object inside every inner helper function
commonMistakes.fix: Validate once at the ingress boundary ("Parse, don’t validate"), then rely on TypeScript internally.

interviewQA.question: What does the engineering mantra "Parse, don’t validate" mean in TypeScript?
interviewQA.answer: Instead of scattered boolean checks that discard proof, parse raw `unknown` input once at the boundary into a strictly typed domain value that downstream code can trust statically.

interviewQA.question: Where in a web app are runtime checks strictly necessary despite strict TypeScript?
interviewQA.answer: HTTP API responses, localStorage/sessionStorage reads, URL search params, postMessage events, and JSON file imports.

lessons.title: Typed Result<T, E> Pattern vs Exceptions
lessons.summary: Because JavaScript `throw` is untyped (TypeScript catch variables are always `unknown`), expected domain failures (validation errors, quiz lockouts, 404s) are often modeled cleanly with a typed `Result<T, E>` discriminated union.
explanation: Because JavaScript `throw` is untyped (TypeScript catch variables are always `unknown`), expected domain failures (validation errors, quiz lockouts, 404s) are often modeled cleanly with a typed `Result<T, E>` discriminated union.
Exceptions stay great for truly unexpected bugs/crashes, while `Result<T, E>` forces callers to explicitly handle known failure modes at compile time.
Use `Result<T, E>` for parsers, form validators, and service boundaries where callers must branch on specific error codes.

codeExample.title: Explicit Error Handling with Result<T, E>

keyPoints: Result<T, E> makes failure modes visible directly in the function’s return type.
Eliminates forgotten try/catch blocks for expected domain errors.
Works seamlessly with discriminated union narrowing (`if (r.ok)`).

commonMistakes.mistake: Wrapping every single one-liner in Result when a crash is genuinely unrecoverable
commonMistakes.fix: Reserve Result for expected, recoverable domain errors; throw Errors for programmer invariant violations.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing raw strings and hoping callers know what error shapes to catch
commonMistakes.fix: Return typed Result unions or documented Error subclasses.

interviewQA.question: Why cannot TypeScript express checked exceptions like Java’s `throws IOException`?
interviewQA.answer: Because JS call stacks and higher-order callbacks can throw arbitrary values anywhere; `Result<T, E>` brings checked-error ergonomics natively to TypeScript.

interviewQA.question: How does narrowing work on `Result<number, string>`?
interviewQA.answer: Checking `if (res.ok)` narrows to `{ ok: true; value: number }`, and the `else` branch narrows to `{ ok: false; error: string }`.

lessons.title: Shared Full-Stack Contracts (API Routes, DTOs & Monorepos)
lessons.summary: Sharing TypeScript types between backend Express/Node handlers and frontend React clients guarantees that renaming a field on the server immediately flags every broken UI call site before deployment.
explanation: Sharing TypeScript types between backend Express/Node handlers and frontend React clients guarantees that renaming a field on the server immediately flags every broken UI call site before deployment.
Define a central `EndpointMap` interface mapping routes to `{ req; res }` pairs so a tiny typed `apiFetch` helper autocompletes both paths and response shapes automatically.
Separate persistence entities (DB rows with Date/internal columns) from serialized JSON DTOs (ISO date strings) at the API contract layer.

codeExample.title: Typed Route-Map Fetch Client

keyPoints: One shared contract types both backend responses and frontend consumers.
Indexed access `ApiRoutes[Path]["res"]` pairs each URL path with its exact response shape.
Remember that `Date` objects serialize to ISO `string` over JSON.

commonMistakes.mistake: Typing a JSON API response field as `createdAt: Date` without deserializing it
commonMistakes.fix: JSON.parse produces strings, not Date instances; type JSON DTO timestamps as `string` (ISO-8601).

commonMistakes.mistake: Duplicating API response interfaces separately in backend/ and frontend/
commonMistakes.fix: Place shared contract types in a shared module imported via `import type`.

interviewQA.question: Why is typing a raw JSON API field as `createdAt: Date` a subtle bug?
interviewQA.answer: JSON has no native Date type, so `res.json()` returns an ISO string; calling `createdAt.getFullYear()` crashes at runtime unless you explicitly parse `new Date(dto.createdAt)`.

interviewQA.question: How does `apiGet<Path extends keyof ApiRoutes>(path: Path)` prevent broken URLs?
interviewQA.answer: Only registered route keys in `ApiRoutes` compile, and the return type automatically matches that exact endpoint’s response type.

lessons.title: Type-Level Testing & Compiler Performance Hygiene
lessons.summary: Complex generic libraries need compile-time tests—using `Expect<Equal<A, B>>` helpers and `// @ts-expect-error` assertions—to guarantee utility types never silently regress to `any`.
explanation: Complex generic libraries need compile-time tests—using `Expect<Equal<A, B>>` helpers and `// @ts-expect-error` assertions—to guarantee utility types never silently regress to `any`.

Keep builds snappy on large repos by annotating exported function return types (aids incremental/isolated declarations), preferring `interface extends` over giant `&` intersections, and checking `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` when builds slow down.
Run `tsc --noEmit` in CI alongside unit tests so zero type regressions ever reach main.

codeExample.title: Compile-Time Type Equality Assertions

keyPoints: `Expect<Equal<A, B>>` verifies exact type equality (even distinguishing `any` from concrete types).
Prefer `interface A extends B` over repeated `{ ... } & { ... }` intersections for faster type checking.
Explicit return types on exported APIs speed up IDE responsiveness and catch accidental API changes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Testing types by only checking assignability (`const x: Target = actual`)
commonMistakes.fix: Assignability misses `any` regressions (`any` is assignable to everything!); use strict `Equal<A, B>`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Exporting deeply inferred 80-line anonymous return types from public modules
commonMistakes.fix: Explicit return annotations keep IDE hints crisp and dramatically speed up incremental compilation.

interviewQA.question: Why is `interface C extends A, B` generally faster for tsc than `type C = A & B`?
interviewQA.answer: Interfaces create a single flat cached object type with explicit conflict checking, whereas intersections are recomputed lazily across usages.

interviewQA.question: How do you test that an invalid call REALLY fails TypeScript compilation?
interviewQA.answer: Place `// @ts-expect-error` directly above the invalid call in a test file—if it accidentally compiles, tsc fails the build!

sections.title: TypeScript 5+ Modern Patterns & Real-World Architecture
sections.description: Use TC39 decorators, `using` explicit resource management, module augmentation, and clean strict migration strategies.

lessons.title: Explicit Resource Management (`using` & `Symbol.dispose`)
lessons.summary: TypeScript 5.2+ supports ECMAScript Explicit Resource Management (`using` and `await using`), deterministically calling `[Symbol.dispose]()` when execution leaves a lexical block—even if an exception is thrown!
explanation: TypeScript 5.2+ supports ECMAScript Explicit Resource Management (`using` and `await using`), deterministically calling `[Symbol.dispose]()` when execution leaves a lexical block—even if an exception is thrown!
Like C#’s `using` or Python’s `with`, this eliminates forgotten `finally` cleanups for database connections, file handles, locks, and AbortControllers.
Implement `[Symbol.dispose]()` on scoped locks, timers, and temporary test fixtures for leak-proof cleanup.

codeExample.title: Deterministic Cleanup with `using` & Disposable

keyPoints: `using` automatically invokes `[Symbol.dispose]()` at the end of the enclosing scope.
`await using` invokes async `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` cleanly.
Guaranteed execution even when early returns or exceptions occur.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `using` without targeting ESNext / polyfilling `Symbol.dispose` in older browsers
commonMistakes.fix: Ensure your runtime (Node 22+ or polyfill) supports `Symbol.dispose` or check target compatibility.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting `DisposableStack` when managing multiple dynamic resources
commonMistakes.fix: Use `new DisposableStack()` to register and dispose multiple resources in LIFO order.

interviewQA.question: What problem does TypeScript 5.2’s `using` keyword solve?
interviewQA.answer: It guarantees deterministic teardown of resources (connections, file descriptors, subscriptions) at scope exit without verbose nested `try / finally` blocks.

interviewQA.question: In what order are multiple `using` resources disposed when leaving a block?
interviewQA.answer: Reverse declaration order (LIFO—last acquired, first disposed), just like C++ RAII and Go defer.

lessons.title: Standard TC39 Decorators in TypeScript 5
lessons.summary: TypeScript 5 implements the finalized Stage 3 ECMAScript Decorators standard—allowing clean, strongly typed method/class/accessor instrumentation without enabling legacy `experimentalDecorators`.
explanation: TypeScript 5 implements the finalized Stage 3 ECMAScript Decorators standard—allowing clean, strongly typed method/class/accessor instrumentation without enabling legacy `experimentalDecorators`.
Standard decorators receive `(target, context)` where `context` provides `kind`, `name`, `access`, and `addInitializer`—making logging, memoization, and method auto-binding 100% type-safe.
Use standard TC39 decorators for new projects; only keep `experimentalDecorators: true` if required by legacy frameworks (e.g., older NestJS/TypeORM metadata).

codeExample.title: Type-Safe Standard TS 5 Method Logger Decorator

keyPoints: TS 5 standard decorators work out of the box without experimental flags.
ClassMethodDecoratorContext gives exact metadata and `addInitializer` hooks.
Generic decorator signatures preserve wrapped method parameters and return types.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing `experimentalDecorators: true` with standard TS 5 decorator signatures
commonMistakes.fix: Legacy and standard decorators have different parameter lists; pick one consistently per tsconfig.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing `this` typing when wrapping a decorated method
commonMistakes.fix: Use a regular `function(this: This, ...args: Args)` (not an arrow function) so `this` binds to the class instance.

interviewQA.question: How do TS 5 standard decorators differ from legacy `experimentalDecorators`?
interviewQA.answer: Standard decorators follow the official TC39 spec with `(value, context)` parameters, do not support parameter decorators or `emitDecoratorMetadata`, and work across all compliant JS runtimes.

interviewQA.question: Why must the wrapper returned by a method decorator be a `function`, not an arrow function?
interviewQA.answer: So `this` binds dynamically to the class instance invoking the method instead of lexically capturing `undefined`.

lessons.title: Module Augmentation & Global Declarations
lessons.summary: Module augmentation (`declare module "express-serve-static-core" { ... }`) cleanly adds custom fields like `req.user` to third-party library interfaces without forking `node_modules`.
explanation: Module augmentation (`declare module "express-serve-static-core" { ... }`) cleanly adds custom fields like `req.user` to third-party library interfaces without forking `node_modules`.

Make sure any `.d.ts` file containing `declare module` includes at least one top-level `import` or `export` (even `export {};`) so TypeScript treats it as an external module augmentation rather than an ambient override!
Place all third-party augmentations in a single well-documented `src/types/augmentations.d.ts` file.

codeExample.title: Safe Module Augmentation Pattern

keyPoints: `export {};` makes a file a module so `declare module` merges instead of overwriting.
`declare global { ... }` safely extends `Window` or `ProcessEnv`.
Keep augmentations minimal and clearly scoped.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `declare module "pkg"` in a file with NO import/export
commonMistakes.fix: Without an import/export, TypeScript treats the file as a script and WIPES OUT the package’s real types!

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating `Array.prototype` globally via `declare global`
commonMistakes.fix: Avoid extending built-in JS prototypes; reserve `declare global` for genuine host globals like `window` or `import.meta.env`.

interviewQA.question: Why is `export {};` required in a `.d.ts` file that uses `declare global`?
interviewQA.answer: Because `declare global` is only valid inside a module file; `export {};` turns a file with no imports into a module cleanly.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you augment a module without making the file a module?
interviewQA.answer: TypeScript treats it as an ambient module declaration that completely shadows the library’s official types.

lessons.title: Migrating JavaScript Codebases to Strict TypeScript
lessons.summary: Migrating a real production JS codebase succeeds best incrementally: enable `allowJs: true`, rename leaf utility files `.js` -> `.ts` first, turn on `strict` flags one by one, and enforce zero new `any` in CI.
explanation: Migrating a real production JS codebase succeeds best incrementally: enable `allowJs: true`, rename leaf utility files `.js` -> `.ts` first, turn on `strict` flags one by one, and enforce zero new `any` in CI.
Start with pure domain utilities and data models (fewest dependencies), then services, then UI components—this unlocks immediate autocomplete benefits across the whole team.
Even before renaming `.js` files, adding `// @ts-check` with JSDoc `@param` annotations catches null bugs immediately with zero build changes.

codeExample.title: Incremental Migration Config Strategy

keyPoints: Migrate bottom-up: leaf utilities -> services -> UI components.
Use `// @ts-check` + JSDoc for zero-risk gradual typing in remaining `.js` files.
Enable `strictNullChecks` early—it catches the highest density of real production crashes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Enabling `"strict": false` permanently after a "big bang" rename to `.ts`
commonMistakes.fix: Strict-off TypeScript hides null bugs and implicit `any`; aim for `strict: true` cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Migrating giant tangled UI components before typing core domain models
commonMistakes.fix: Type core domain interfaces first so every component consuming them immediately gains type checking.

interviewQA.question: In what order should you migrate files in a large JS codebase to TypeScript?
interviewQA.answer: Bottom-up: start with shared types and leaf utility modules that have the fewest internal imports, then services/API clients, and finally top-level UI pages.

interviewQA.question: What does `// @ts-check` at the top of a `.js` file do?
interviewQA.answer: It instructs TypeScript to type-check that JavaScript file using inference and JSDoc annotations without renaming it to `.ts`.
